Ezra Pound. The American poet, critic, and literary impresario whose ambition was to make it new—to radically renew poetry by mining the full archive of world literature.

Born in Idaho in 1885, Pound studied at Penn and Hamilton College, always seeking European cultural authority. He settled in London in 1908, then Paris and Italy, forever an outsider. As a poetry editor and critic, he discovered and mentored James Joyce, T. S. Eliot, and Robert Frost. His recommendations launched careers and shaped the course of modernism itself. He founded and promoted Imagism in the early nineteen-tens, a movement emphasizing clarity, precision, and direct presentation of images over Victorian sentimentality. Yet his later career took a troubling turn. He became increasingly interested in economics, monetary theory, and politics, eventually embracing fascism. He supported Mussolini, made wartime broadcasts on Rome Radio, and was arrested for treason in 1945, then confined to an asylum.

His major works include Personae, published in 1909, a collection of early poems including "The River Merchant's Wife: A Letter," a famous translation-pastiche. Hugh Selwyn Mauberley appeared in 1920, a sequence of short poems reflecting on modernism, World War I, and artistic failure. Compressed and allusive, it stands as one of his most accessible achievements. His life's work, The Cantos, began in 1917 and was never finished. These 120 cantos form a collaged verse of fragments—history, economics, myth, and autobiography all jumbled together. The poem jumps between languages and centuries, drawing on Dante, Homer, Confucius, and Chinese ideograms. It is notoriously difficult and uneven.

Pound's aesthetic is defined by his imperative to make it new—to break from the past by absorbing and reinventing it. Deep learning paired with radical experimentation. Imagism demands precise, economic language; concrete images; no unnecessary words. He draws on Japanese poetry and classical brevity. His collage technique mixes high and low, ancient and modern, translation and original composition. Meaning emerges from juxtaposition. Allusion functions as method: knowledge of Dante, Homer, Confucius, and Chinese ideograms is embedded in the poem itself. Readability requires scholarship.

Pound is the exemplary modernist maker—the artist as cultural entrepreneur, editor, and network-builder. He gave shape to the modernist movement by recognizing talent and pushing artists toward formal innovation. Yet his legacy is haunted. His anti-Semitism and fascist politics are indefensible, raising the question of whether great art can redeem a reprehensible life. The Cantos stands as simultaneously modernism's most ambitious poem and dismissed as unreadable chaos. Pound represents modernism's revolutionary potential and its ethical blind spots—a figure one must know without endorsing.
